label: prop:binding-functional-is-the-log
title: Only the logarithmic binding functional is extensive; the linear rival fails by $-\alpha(1-x)(1-y)$ and carries a ceiling
html:
Proposition. Only the logarithmic binding functional is extensive; the linear rival fails by -\alpha(1-x)(1-y) and carries a ceiling

Proposition. Write t for a trace ratio and \alpha > 0 for the energy scale. The logarithmic functional B = -\alpha \ln t is extensive,

  -\alpha \ln(xy) \;=\; -\alpha \ln x \;+\; -\alpha \ln y
  \qquad (x, y > 0),

while the linear functional B = \alpha(1 - t) fails extensivity by an exact amount,

  \alpha(1 - xy) - \bigl[\alpha(1-x) + \alpha(1-y)\bigr]
    \;=\; -\alpha\,(1-x)(1-y),

which vanishes only when x = 1 or y = 1. Separately, since the atom trace is positive, \alpha(t_{\mathrm{free}} - t_{\mathrm{atom}}) < \alpha\,t_{\mathrm{free}}.

The Markov trace is multiplicative over independent subsystems, so an atom's trace factors as t_{\mathrm{atom}} = t_{\mathrm{free}} \prod_k \mu_k over its bonds. Energy, on the other hand, is extensive. A map carrying the first structure to the second must send products to sums — Cauchy's equation on (\mathbb{R}_{>0}, \times) — whose continuous solutions are the multiples of \ln.

The proposition records the part of that argument which is mechanically checkable: of the two functionals the framework has weighed, the logarithmic one is extensive and the linear one is not. The failure is stated as an identity rather than as a measurement, so it holds at every q and needs no anchor; a bond with x = 1 contributes nothing, so on any bond that binds at all the linear form is non-extensive.

The ceiling is an independent objection and does not rely on extensivity at all. With t_{\mathrm{free}} \approx 1 across the light nuclei, the linear form cannot produce a binding energy above \alpha \approx 4.19\ \mathrm{MeV}, which already excludes {}^{3}\mathrm{H}, {}^{4}\mathrm{He} and {}^{7}\mathrm{Li} against their measured values. Two separate reasons therefore point the same way.

Scope. The uniqueness step — that Cauchy's equation admits no continuous solutions beyond c \ln x — is classical and is not formalised here, so the stronger reading, that the logarithmic form is forced rather than merely preferred among the two candidates, rests on it. What is proved is the comparison. Nothing here bears on the value of \alpha, which is fixed elsewhere, nor on whether the trace ratio entering the formula is the right one.
